title: Measuring What Matters: Developing Human-Centered Legal Q-and-A Quality Standards through Multi-Stakeholder Research
pub: JURIX 2024 AI for Access to Justice Workshop; SSRN 5146722
author: Margaret Hagan

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Cheaper assistance: More participation may not yield remedies
st.an: The supplied material is bibliographic only. Although it identifies literature on human-centred legal-AI quality and reliability, it provides no substantive claims or findings showing whether the source accepts, rejects or extends the cluster’s proposition that cheaper assistance and increased participation may not produce effective remedies.
qs: Hagan, Towards Human-Centered Standards for Legal Help AI, Philosophical Transactions      of the Royal Society A (2024).

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The supplied evidence consists only of bibliography fragments. Although the cited literature concerns legal-service quality, AI evaluation, hallucinations and human-centered standards, it does not disclose the source’s own findings or position on bounded workflows, verification, competence risks, lawyer replacement or deployment practices.

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI, including RAG systems, can produce hallucinated legal information, while materially extending the cluster’s governance framing: legal Q-and-A quality should be assessed not only for accuracy and hallucinations but also through stakeholder-informed standards focused on consumers’ legal and life outcomes.
qs: Rather than presuming to know what matters when evaluating Legal Q-and-A, this paper proposes that researchers must first consult stakeholders with front-line experience with what answers improve consumers’ legal and life outcomes.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s selective, human-led deployment model and materially extends it for consumer legal Q-and-A. It positions AI as an initial navigator rather than a complete legal solution, then develops a participatory, domain-specific evaluation framework centred on legal and jurisdictional accuracy, actionability, accessibility, context and user outcomes—not accuracy or hallucination detection alone.
qs: The desired role for AI is a helpful navigator of high-quality information and resources, that provides a good initial orientation, but that is not the full legal expert itself.
If AI is ^Lto have human-centered outcomes, its development and evaluation cycles must be built around the knowledge of users and provider experts in a given domain.

st.t: Legal benchmarks: Realistic tasks expose uneven competence
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that legal-AI evaluation must be realistic and task-specific, while benchmark conclusions remain contingent on coverage and grading choices. It particularly reinforces the identified gap in consumer-facing evaluation: corporate-oriented benchmarks poorly represent everyday legal problems, and comparison with human answers does not itself establish whether guidance is helpful or harmful.
qs: Aside from one benchmark for issue-spotting common legal issues in r/legaladvice posts in Legal Bench, the benchmarks primarily concern tasks and standards that are more complex than the everyday problems that consumers ask for help with.
It did not, however, conduct research into what criteria make an answer helpful or harmful.

st.t: Legal-help evaluation: Resolved problems outrank exam accuracy
st.an: The source directly endorses evaluating consumer legal AI by whether it helps resolve everyday legal problems and avoids harmful life outcomes, rather than by accuracy alone. It also treats its human-centered, multi-stakeholder rubric as an initial framework for future evaluation, not evidence of demonstrated access-to-justice gains.
qs: example, determining the accuracy of the legal analysis contained in the answer), this paper argues that researchers must talk to people with lived experience in doing the Q-and-A task as providers or as users, to understand what about this task matters most in their key outcome: resolving the legal problem and avoiding bad life outcomes around their home, finances, family, and employment.
The rubric is an initial contribution that helps technologists, researchers, and regulators know what to measure.

kp.k: Consumer legal AI needs standards beyond legal accuracy
kp.d: Hagan argues that consumer legal question-answering lacks a systematic, reliable quality protocol. Accuracy and absence of hallucinations matter but cannot alone establish whether an answer helps someone resolve an everyday legal problem or avoid harm. The proposed alternative defines quality through users' and frontline providers' experience, particularly in landlord-tenant matters.
qs: A definition of quality anchored only on legal accuracy risks missing other key needs that a person has, and that a good Legal Q-and-A interaction can provide them with.
It also risks missing harms that may occur even if the Legal Q-and-A provides a hallucination-free, accurate legal analysis.

kp.k: Undefined quality can distort regulation of new services
kp.d: Drawing on prior legal-services scholarship, the paper argues that absent explicit standards, policymakers may judge technology against an idealized version of expert human services using anecdotal assessments. Hagan presents this as a potential chilling effect on innovation, rather than reporting a newly measured regulatory effect.
qs: This absence of quality standards can have a chilling effect on technology innovation.
Technology’s performance is then judged by anecdotal assessments or comparisons to a mythical standard, leading to prohibitions or intense regulation.

kp.k: Three studies ground the proposed evaluation framework
kp.d: The Legal Design Lab describes an 18-month, three-study sequence: interviews with 46 community members between June 2023 and February 2024, including fictional eviction exercises using Google Bard or ChatGPT when participants agreed; 45-minute Zoom interviews with 21 experts in November 2023 rating 22 criteria on a 0–6 scale; and 30-minute Zoom sessions with 21 experts in January–February 2024 evaluating GPT 3.5 answers through Learned Hands. The evidence combines ratings and qualitative comments, not demonstrated improvements in actual legal outcomes. One methods sentence inconsistently refers to four studies.
qs: Over 18 months, the Legal Design Lab conducted 3 sequential studies to establish community-driven quality metrics for Legal Q-and-A.
Participants were asked to rate the importance of each criterion on a scale of 0-6, from not important at all to highly important.
Next to this input, they saw an answer that had been generated by an AI system (OpenAI’s GPT 3.5).

kp.d: The author explicitly characterizes the 46-person user sample as a limited convenience sample, recruited through courthouse intercepts, social media ads, Qualtrics research services, and family-and-friends recruitment. All 29 courthouse participants lived in California; the 17 online participants were comfortable participating in Internet research. The paper presents these interviews as initial evidence of themes, not representative estimates for American adults.
qs: We recognize that the limited convenience sample of 46 community members is not representative of all American adults.
Our 29 in-person intercept interviews at courthouses were all for participants who live in California.
Our 17 online interviews were with participants who were comfortable using the Internet to participate in online research.

kp.k: Users envision AI as orientation, not complete representation
kp.d: Several community participants viewed AI as an initial navigator supplying issue identification, action plans, referrals, and encouragement rather than comprehensive legal research or a complete legal solution. This is a finding about participants' desired role for consumer AI, not evidence that AI substitutes for lawyers across legal services.
qs: The desired role for AI is a helpful navigator of high-quality information and resources, that provides a good initial orientation, but that is not the full legal expert itself.
The users were not expecting comprehensive legal research or analysis of their case.

kp.k: Useful answers require accessible, local, actionable information
kp.d: Users valued concise organization, rapid understanding of their problem, current jurisdiction-specific rules, deadlines, forms, and practical next steps. Experts broadly reinforced accuracy, readability, and actionability. Appendix B places plain language, no substantive-law misrepresentations, no legal-form misrepresentations, and no toxicity in its highest, 6-out-of-6 importance category.
qs: They criticized answers that gave generic and high-level information as unhelpful and discouraging.
The community members saw little value in answers that did not have these local, detailed action steps about forms, deadlines, service referrals, or descriptions of rights.
Plain language and accessible information design were also ranked as highly important by the experts.

kp.k: Experts identified potentially harmful procedural errors
kp.d: In Study 3, experts identified outdated eviction-lawsuit time periods, incorrect eviction-warning notice periods, and an incorrect court system in sample AI answers. They emphasized procedural accuracy because missed deadlines or incorrect paperwork can damage cases. These are qualitative observations of sample answers; the paper does not supply a model-wide error rate.
qs: Several experts in Study 3 found accuracy errors, particularly around the timelines and time periods that the answer was providing.
Experts found out-of-date eviction lawsuit time periods (E3); the required time for an eviction warning notice (E18, E20); and the incorrect court system being named (E8).
Experts have seen people lose their cases because they did not follow the correct procedural timeline or paperwork.

kp.k: Generic lawyer referrals may fail underserved users
kp.d: Users and experts criticized instructions to consult an attorney without usable pathways to affordable assistance. Experts reviewing answers wanted specific local legal-aid, law-library, or other low-cost resources. Their concern is access to justice: referrals should be feasible for people unable to afford or obtain counsel, rather than merely direct them away from AI.
qs: As experts looked at actual AI answers in Study 3, many emphasized the importance of giving clear referrals to find a low-cost or free local legal help provider.
Many other experts flagged as unhelpful when an answer encouraged people to speak to a legal expert but did not give actionable guidance to do so.

kp.k: Disclaimers attracted disagreement and concerns about discouraging action
kp.d: In Study 2, two experts rated a consult-a-lawyer disclaimer 6 out of 6 and four rated it 5 out of 6. Most cautioned against overweighting disclaimers; some regarded them as serving professional risk aversion or company liability rather than user needs. Experts warned that excessive warnings could paralyze users or discourage assertion of rights. These are participant assessments, not measured causal effects.
qs: In Study 2, two respondents rated it 6 out of 6, and four rated it 5 out of 6 importance.
Most respondents, though, cautioned against putting too much value on disclaimers.
Several experts cautioned that warnings and disclaimers can hurt a person, discouraging them from pursuing their legal rights

kp.k: Citations support verification but can overwhelm users
kp.d: Community members valued links and citations for checking accuracy and currency, pursuing further research, and demonstrating legal rights to an opposing party. Several experts gave primary-law citations lower priority because they could confuse users; others recognized their verification value. The paper favors concise links as practical tools rather than citation-heavy answers.
qs: A final recurrent theme around helpfulness and harm was the AI’s provision of citations, links, or other ways that the user could verify its content was accurate.
A final group of respondents valued citations for a different reason: to use them as a tool for negotiation with the party they are in conflict with.
But this citation should be brief and concise, more of a tool than a load of information.

kp.k: Comprehensive analysis must be balanced against usable next steps
kp.d: Experts cautioned that detailed, comprehensive legal analysis can overwhelm people and reduce engagement. They sought a balance between adequate specificity and a coherent, concise plan. Hagan distinguishes this consumer-support task from corporate-lawyer research: deprioritizing exhaustive analysis does not mean accepting inaccurate procedural or substantive guidance.
qs: Several experts warned that robustness should not be given too much weight, because detailed legal analyses can become overwhelming and off-putting.
A robust, detailed examination of the law and how it applies to the person’s scenario may be a common task for a corporate lawyer, but it is not what most people want from an answer.
Instead, they want service referrals, timelines, form and document links, and advice on what works in practice to resolve a problem.

kp.k: Draft rubric separates helpful features from potential harms
kp.d: The synthesis proposes four positive categories—Legal Analysis, Actionable Plan, Empowerment, and Strategic Caution—and three negative categories—Misrepresentations, Bias, and Toxicity. Weighted scoring and regular audits are envisioned future implementations for universities, regulators, and technology companies, not an already validated scoring system. The supplied document includes an Appendix E figure caption but no readable rubric figure details.
qs: The positive quality criteria are in 4 categories: (1) Legal Analysis; (2) Actionable Plan; (3) Empowerment; and (4) Strategic Caution.
The negative criteria are in 3 categories: (1) Misrepresentations; (2) Bias; and (3) Toxicity.
We envision a future scoring system that can give AI answers weighted points for the positive criteria they include, and subtract for the negative criteria they include.

kp.k: Participatory evaluation should shape legal AI development
kp.d: Hagan recommends extending the multi-stakeholder method to other legal tasks. The argument is that evaluation standards influence developers' fine-tuning and policymakers' rules and funding, so measures should reflect domain users' and providers' knowledge rather than convenient proxies alone. This is a recommendation and proposed mechanism, not a measured market forecast.
qs: How AI is measured will affect how AI develops.
Measurement benchmarks will steer assessments used by policymakers to set rules and funding around AI, and used by technology developers as they evaluate and finetune their systems.
We recommend a similar multi-stakeholder process to establish human-centered quality evaluation standards for other tasks in the legal domain, aside from Q-and-A.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Hagan anticipates increasing consumer use of AI for legal problem-solving and identifies its desired role as initial orientation rather than comprehensive legal representation.
pts.d: The adoption statement is a qualitative expectation, not a quantified forecast. Based on community-member interviews, Hagan describes a preferred service role: identifying issues, providing an action plan, and directing users to forms and providers. This is a finding about users' expectations and perceived utility, not evidence that AI replaces lawyers or resolves cases successfully.

pts.k: Hagan argues that accurate legal analysis alone does not establish whether consumer-facing AI legal help is helpful or safe.
pts.d: Her synthesis emphasizes accurate, locally relevant, current information combined with readable presentation, actionable next steps, empowerment, and referrals. Experts reviewing GPT-3.5 answers identified procedural inaccuracies, including outdated eviction periods and incorrect courts. Hagan links such mistakes to potential harm through experts' experience of procedural failures; the study does not report actual case losses caused by its tested answers.

pts.k: Interviewed experts warn that generic lawyer referrals, strong disclaimers, and overly comprehensive answers can undermine AI's usefulness for people seeking affordable legal help.
pts.d: These are attributed practitioner judgments, not measured causal effects. R13 warns that disclaimers can discourage action; R9 connects ineffective referrals to insufficient lawyer availability; E20 considers advice to seek counsel unhelpful without concrete resources. Some experts nevertheless rated disclaimers highly. Experts also caution that detailed legal analysis may overwhelm users, favoring a balance between specificity and accessible next steps.

pts.k: Users describe citations and links as enabling verification, further research, and more credible negotiation; experts qualify their value by warning against overwhelming users.
pts.d: Hagan reports that users wanted ways to check accuracy and currency before relying on AI answers. Participant P1 also expected legal links to help demonstrate rights to a landlord. These are desired benefits rather than demonstrated improvements in negotiation outcomes. Several experts favored concise links over extensive case or statutory discussion.

pts.k: Hagan predicts that evaluation standards will shape AI development and regulation, and proposes participatory standards to steer consumer legal AI toward useful outcomes.
pts.d: Hagan argues that poorly chosen measures can misrepresent benefits and harms, while human-centered measures can guide system improvement and policy. Drawing on prior legal-quality scholarship, she also argues that absent standards can chill innovation by encouraging anecdotal comparisons with idealized human services. Her proposed rubric and future weighted scoring system are evaluation infrastructure proposals, not a validated benchmark or demonstrated intervention.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The primary evidence is a mixed-methods sequence involving 46 community members and two expert studies of 21 participants each.
pts.d: Study 1 combined interviews, a fictional eviction scenario, and optional use of Bard or ChatGPT. Study 2 asked justice professionals to rate 22 quality criteria on a 0–6 scale and explain their judgments. Study 3 elicited expert ratings and commentary on GPT-3.5 eviction answers through Learned Hands. The evidence supports reported preferences, practitioner concerns, and observed sample-answer problems; it does not establish population adoption rates, quantified model error rates, or improved legal outcomes. Hagan draws separately on prior scholarship about legal-service quality and cites legal hallucination research rather than presenting those studies' findings as her own measurements.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The empirical observations concern 2023–2024 exercises, while adoption growth and rubric implementation are prospective and undated.
pts.d: Community interviews ran June 2023–February 2024; the criteria-ranking study occurred in November 2023; expert answer-rating interviews occurred January–February 2024. The paper describes the broader research sequence as spanning 18 months. Findings focus on consumer landlord-tenant questions, especially fictional eviction scenarios. Community evidence is qualified by convenience sampling: 29 in-person participants lived in California and 17 online participants were comfortable participating in Internet research. Benefits depend on accurate local procedures, usable content, feasible referrals, and appropriately balanced detail. The rubric remains an initial contribution requiring future operationalization and testing.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are consumers with everyday civil legal needs, frontline legal-help providers, AI developers, researchers, and regulators.
pts.d: For consumers, particularly tenants and people unable to obtain affordable counsel, AI may offer initial navigation, practical next steps, and routes to help, but may also mislead or discourage action. Legal aid staff, court help centers, librarians, and other justice professionals contribute domain experience and are potential referral destinations. Developers could use the rubric to improve systems; researchers and government bodies could use it to audit benefits and harms. The paper distinguishes these consumer needs from corporate legal research and makes no concrete prediction about law-firm staffing, lawyer displacement, billing, or legal-market shares.
